newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY UNION - Hart lashes out at South Africans.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION - Hart lashes out at South Africans.

text.p: PRETORIA, July 17 - The buildup for Sunday's (NZ time) rugby tri-series opener has turned ugly as All Black coach John Hart claimed hysteria and desperation would drive South Africa to indulge in intimidation and illegalities at Ellis Park, NZPA reports.

Hart said he would talk to match referee, Australian Peter Marshall, to make him aware of South Africa's likely physical intimidation on and off the ball, and their habit of slowing down play through faked injuries and other illegal methods.

The All Black camp are genuinely worried that some of their young stars will be targeted for rough treatment and that jealousy has already triggered an orchestrated effort by the Springboks to influence the referee.
For those reasons, Hart said his team's entire preparation this week had been based around discipline. But he warned that the All Blacks were not prepared to take a step back on Sunday.

The coach's unusual attack, the strongest heard from him since he took over the All Blacks last season, comes amid constant reminders from the South Africans, and before them the Australians, about the All Blacks' alleged use of professional
fouls.
Wallabies coach Greg Smith accused the All Blacks of employing the tactic in their 30-13 first Bledisloe Cup test win in Christchurch two weeks ago.
Australian Rugby Union chief executive John O'Neill also launched a scathing attack on English referee Ed Morrison, who had controlled the Bledisloe Cup match.

O'Neill openly accused Morrison of being "matey" with the All Blacks and said he would have severe words with the referee before the second match in Melbourne next week. Morrison will control that test also.
"It's disappointing really," Hart said of O'Neill's criticism.
After reprimanding lock Robin Brooke for one professional foul, Hart said he had watched the video of the game and found that the Australians had used the same tactic on at least three occasions.
In South Africa, Springbok coach Carel du Plessis and his vice-captain and halfback Joost van der Westhuizen latched on to O'Neill's barbs.
Du Plessis said he would speak to Marshall regarding the All Blacks' tactics and van der Westhuizen suggested his team should employ professional fouls to counter the All Blacks'.
The South African media today highlighted du Plessis' and van der Westhuizen's comments.
Hart counter-attacked, saying he would have a word with Marshall over three main issues.
"This publicity about professional fouls -- my coaching approach is never to condone them. I just want to understand if he (Marshall) has any issues with us and if there are, we'll address them.

"The second thing is the fact that I think the Springboks will try to physically intimidate us on and off the ball. I hope that we're aware of that and the referee and the touch judges watch that because I think in their last test against the British Lions (two weeks ago) there were some really marginal stuff that got let go, which I don't think has a place in the game.

"And the third thing is that I think that because of the pack they've (Springboks) picked, which is immensely big, has a danger of being a little slower and not quite as athletic as the All Blacks pack. That means they will try to slow the game down
by (faking) injuries and other methods so they can get to set pieces and then start the game again at their own pace.
"Even though we're playing at altitude, we'll be looking at playing at pace."
Hart said intimidation and specific targets to take a player out of a match had no place in the sport.
"But you've got to be concerned here in terms of their need to win and they may possibly do that (take a player out)."
He believed that the Australians and the South Africans were resorting to influence the referees because they could not find another way of beating the All Blacks.
